item.title: Stocks Tumble as Democrats Are Set to Gain Control of Congress
item.description:
Asian stock markets tumbled on Wednesday as Democrats appeared poised to take control of Congress, raising concerns that greater scrutiny of the data center boom could derail a prolonged rally in the region’s technology stocks.

The S&P 500 futures fell 1.1 percent in after-hours trading, while losses swept across Asian markets. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 plunged 3.6 percent to its lowest intraday level in three months. Taiwan’s stock index sank 3 percent, also hitting a three-month low. South Korea’s KOSPI index dropped 2.9 percent.

In recent days, betting markets had favored a Democratic victory in the House, though the Senate remained a closer contest. But as the early results appeared to indicate a landslide victory for Democrats in the House and Senate, it provided more clarity on how the shift in Washington might affect U.S. policy toward artificial intelligence and the vast sums being poured into data centers.

Many of Asia’s major equities markets have outperformed their American and European counterparts for much of the year, powered by relatively attractive valuations but driven primarily by booming demand for A.I. hardware.

A Democratic sweep now threatens to disrupt that momentum.

“The sell-off in Asia today is because of A.I.,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at the investment bank Natixis.

While investors fear that greater Democratic oversight could slow data-center investment, Ms. Garcia-Herrero said she did not expect the party to “kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.”

“The market is reading chaos,” Ms. Garcia-Herrero added. “I don’t think Trump is going to sit and say, ‘Wonderful.’ That’s not him. So the market is preparing for bad news in terms of Trump reacting to all of this.”

In an interview with The New York Times, Mr. Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and was prepared to work with Democrats.

The sell-off was particularly pronounced among semiconductor companies that have powered Asia’s stock market gains this year.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company fell 1.1 percent. In South Korea, memory chip manufacturers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dropped 5.4 percent and 3.5 percent, respectively.

In Japan, shares of SoftBank Group, a major technology investor, plunged more than 8 percent, while chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron lost more than 6 percent.

A clean sweep by the Democrats could constrain Mr. Trump’s domestic agenda and “there will be a lot more focus on foreign policy,” said Deepali Bhargava, the chief economist for Asia-Pacific for ING Bank.

“In that sense, Iran escalation and what happens to oil prices is a key risk,” Ms. Bhargava said. “Then, it’s really not good news for Asia.”

Asian markets are already contending with volatile oil prices from the war in the Middle East as well as concerns about U.S. government borrowing that pushed Treasury yields to multidecade highs in September.

The prospect of political gridlock also weighed on the dollar, as investors expected a divided government to curb federal spending and ease some upward pressure on bond yields.

An index measuring the dollar against a basket of currencies fell 0.5 percent on Wednesday, while yields on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note were little changed.

Ms. Bhargava said a blue sweep could put some further pressure on the dollar in the near term. Over a longer horizon, the currency’s direction would remain closely tied to the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decisions.

Historically, stocks have performed well with a divided Congress, because a divided government is seen as a check on sweeping policy changes. But with U.S. borrowing costs already elevated, that conventional wisdom may no longer hold.

“Shutdowns, debt-ceiling brinkmanship and budget gridlock under a Democratic Congress are greater risks,” strategists at the research arm of Amundi Investment Solutions wrote in a report last month. “In prior cycles, gridlock was a relief trade. At current yield levels, it may not be.”

A Democratic-controlled Congress could mean more investigations into Mr. Trump and a possible impeachment, adding another layer of political uncertainty.

For Asian investors, China presents another wild card.

Democrats could take a harder line on Beijing, complicating Mr. Trump’s friendly overtures to China’s leader, Xi Jinping. Mr. Trump’s own approach remains unpredictable. He has alternated between seeking closer ties with Beijing and attacking China over the U.S. trade deficit and alleged currency manipulation.

The midterm results come at a fragile moment for technology stocks. Financial results showing accelerating capital spending helped send shares of Meta and Amazon sharply lower last week, underscoring growing concerns about elevated A.I. investment.

River Akira Davis contributed reporting.

item.title: Candy and Smiles on MS NOW, and Some Regrets on Fox News
item.description:
It was a night when cable news seemed to turn on its head.

The “celebration can absolutely begin,” declared Rachel Maddow just after 10 p.m. Eastern on MS NOW, where she and a band of beaming liberal pundits had just projected a Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives.

Two years ago, back when the network was called MSNBC, hangdog faces dominated as President Trump clinched one battleground state after the next. On Tuesday, Chris Hayes was looking giddy.

“There are races on the board right now that have no business whatsoever of being close,” he said, marveling at the reach of a blue wave that was sweeping even obscure Democratic candidates into Congress. “I’ve never seen these people’s names before! The Democrat — I’m like, ‘Who’s this dude?’”

It wasn’t long until actual candy was being passed around on set, and that was before the Democrats were projected to win the Senate, too. “The miasma of sugar coming off you guys!” Ms. Maddow said, teasingly, as Nicolle Wallace and Michael Steele giggled and acknowledged they had been sneaking some sweets.

Over on Fox News, the mood was subdued. The buoyancy of Mr. Trump’s 2024 election night was replaced with pensive exchanges about what it meant for the Republican Party to be repudiated so starkly.

In a rare concession, Sean Hannity, perhaps Mr. Trump’s most loyal television defender, acknowledged that the president’s foreign policy had proven politically unsound. Asked by Bret Baier if the war in Iran had changed the night’s outcome, Mr. Hannity replied: “One hundred percent. I don’t think there’s any doubt about it.”

He described the shock defeat of Darline Graham, the Republican candidate for Senate in South Carolina, as “brutal.”

Laura Ingraham, another staunch Trump ally, called the American military intervention in Iran “really tough, and not well explained.” She added: “The people just don’t like war. They do not want to go to war.”

A number of Fox pundits invoked “history,” arguing that incumbent presidents frequently face tough midterm losses and implying that Mr. Trump did not deserve blame.

“The more dominant of a personality that a president is, the more dramatic of a loss in the midterm,” Mr. Hannity said, citing Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton. “There is an ebb and flow.”

Karoline Leavitt, Mr. Trump’s former press secretary and now a Fox News contributor, complained that “the mainstream media wouldn’t cover” the president’s perceived achievements. (Another former press secretary, Dana Perino, interjected that Mr. Trump deserved some blame for not selling his agenda.)

Ms. Leavitt was quick to add that Fox News was an exception. But one notable network viewer may not have agreed.

Earlier on Tuesday, Mr. Trump repeatedly lashed out at Fox News, calling its polling results “the worst” and claiming its ratings were “way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!”

At one point, he texted complaints directly to Greg Gutfeld, a co-host of “The Five,” who read his comments on the air. And shortly before midnight, Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social that “Fox News bears responsibilities for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition.”

None of that stopped Mr. Trump from then calling in to Fox for a live on-air interview. He talked with Mr. Baier and Martha MacCallum for roughly half an hour.

Across all the broadcast and cable networks, it was apparent in the early hours of Tuesday’s coverage that the results were headed in one direction. Just before 9 p.m., as CNN’s John King zoomed in on House races in Ohio on his “Magic Wall” map, he told viewers, “Your eyes don’t lie.”

“That’s just a whole lot of blue,” Mr. King added.

Network executives were anticipating high interest for this year’s midterms. NBC announced it would provide 13 consecutive hours of coverage to its affiliates, more than doubling its coverage from election night in 2022.

NBC’s livestream of its data analyst Steve Kornacki punching at his touch-screen monitor turned into an instant hit. The YouTube stream of the “Kornacki Cam” had 335,000 viewers watching at one point, with commenters expressing their admiration of the NBC map man.

“im getting a kornacki tattoo in the morning,” one wrote. “Vote yes on prop Kornacki!” said another.

The MS NOW crew was enjoying itself, too. At one point, Ms. Maddow stepped away from the set; when she returned, she discovered that the channel’s decision desk had declared the Senate races in Ohio, South Carolina and Texas were all headed in the Democrats’ direction.

“I was gone for like 30 seconds,” Ms. Maddow said, to a chorus of laughter. “Would you like me to go away again?”

item.title: Shares of Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX Tumble After Republicans Are Routed
item.description:
Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections. After Democrats claimed sweeping victories, claiming both houses of Congress and other important state races, shares of SpaceX and Tesla, which are both run by Mr. Musk, fell sharply in premarket trading on Wednesday.

Tesla’s stock was down more than 4.5 percent before markets opened, while SpaceX was down 5 percent, dropping below $135, the price it sold shares for in its blockbuster public offering in June. The declines stood out among tech stocks, as Nvidia, Meta, Google and the wider stock market rallied before the official start of trading.

SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger, which could be complicated by a Congress controlled by Democrats, some of whom have already signaled their intent to investigate the world’s richest person and his companies. In recent years, Mr. Musk has antagonized Democrats, spending heavily to elect President Trump, involving himself deeply in the federal government and aligning his companies’ interests with those of the current presidential administration.

“They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Edward J. Markey, a Democrat in Massachusetts, posted on X on Tuesday night about potential hearings for technology executives.

Mr. Musk spent at least $474 million on the midterm election, the most money of any donor in a U.S. election cycle, apart from candidates who have funded their own runs for office. About $224 million was spent on races in Texas, particularly in support of the losing campaign of Ken Paxton for a Senate seat against James Talarico.

Both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered in Texas. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Mr. Musk moved there after declaring that California had become too liberal for his taste.

Both companies are developing extensive infrastructure in Texas, including a joint effort to build a more than $100 billion chip manufacturing plant in the state, though those efforts could now face greater scrutiny. Texas is set to have a Democratic governor after the election of Gina Hinojosa, as well as a Democratic Attorney General and Lieutenant Governor.

Mr. Musk, 55, did not immediately return a request for comment.

Mr. Musk’s midterm spending, while substantial, will have little impact on his overall wealth. As of Tuesday, he was worth $898 billion, according to Bloomberg, meaning that his political contributions amounted to a tiny sliver of his net worth.

In relative terms, it was akin to a 55-year-old with the median U.S. net worth of about $411,000 spending a little more than $217.

Mr. Musk, who avoided posting on X for most of Tuesday night as votes were being counted, returned to his social media platform in the early hours of Wednesday to joke about his political losses and his companies’ prospects.

“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote, referring to SpaceX’s goal to put A.I. computing clusters in orbit.

Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
item.description:
CVS Health plans to split in two, in a major unraveling of the country’s largest health care conglomerate after years of rampant expansion, the company announced on Wednesday.

Under the breakup, planned for the first half of 2028, a new spinoff company, to be called CVS Pharmacy, will house the conglomerate’s approximately 9,000 retail pharmacies, in-store clinics and a warehouse-based operation that sends prescriptions through the mail.

A second company will retain the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefit manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.

CVS Health has been under mounting scrutiny from lawmakers, regulators and others who say the company — along with its peers, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna — has grown too dominant. Critics say the conglomerates have exploited conflicts to profit from their web of businesses, driving up medical costs and stifling competition.

Within the past two years, Arkansas and Tennessee have each passed laws that aim to prevent the conglomerates from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies. In Washington and other states, lawmakers from both parties have proposed similar legislation, which the conglomerates have fiercely opposed.

CVS Health generated over $400 billion in revenue last year. That ranked seventh among U.S. public companies, according to FactSet, a financial data provider.

The Financial Times on Tuesday reported the company’s plans to split itself up.

The planned breakup would end a nearly decade-long chapter in which CVS Health reached into nearly every corner of the health care system. That era began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged. That same year, Cigna bought Express Scripts, the pharmacy benefit manager.

Since then, CVS, UnitedHealth and Cigna have increasingly touched more pieces of the machinery by which Americans receive health care. Each company now encompasses a major insurer, a giant pharmacy benefit manager and a mail-order pharmacy, along with a vast array of other businesses. Critics complain that the conglomerates use their size and leverage to steer patients toward their own pharmacies.

But for CVS, merging its businesses have not met Wall Street’s demands for growth. At the end of 2024, the company’s market value fell to its lowest level in over a decade, though it has since rebounded.

Many investors see CVS’s pharmacy benefit manager as the shining jewel of the portfolio. But prospects have dimmed for the pharmacy business, amid changing consumer habits and industry-wide challenges that have shuttered other major pharmacy chains like Rite Aid.

item.title: The New York Times Adds 420,000 Digital Subscribers
item.description:
The New York Times Company said on Wednesday that it had added 420,000 digital-only subscribers in the third quarter, boosting its total number of paid subscribers to 13.8 million.

The results keep the company roughly on pace to meet its stated goal of 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027 across the news report as well as Wirecutter, Cooking, Games and the Athletic sports news site. The company has added about 1.46 million digital-only subscribers in the past 12 months, though it had a slower second quarter with the addition of 280,000 subscribers.

Total revenue for the third quarter was $768.5 million, an increase of 9.7 percent from the same time period last year. Adjusted operating profit was $149.6 million, up from $131.4 million in the third quarter of last year.

Adjusted operating costs were $618.9 million, an increase of 8.7 percent year over year, which the company said was due to higher compensation and benefits expenses, higher general and administrative costs, and higher marketing and promotion costs. The company had forecast an increase of 8 to 9 percent.

Revenue from digital-only subscriptions grew 14.6 percent year over year, to $421.3 million for the quarter. Digital-only average revenue per user, a metric used to measure the health of subscription businesses, was $9.93, up slightly from the same time last year.

But print subscriptions continued to fall. The Times now has 540,000 print subscribers, down from 570,000 a year earlier.

Digital advertising revenue was up 12 percent to $109.9 million. Revenue from affiliate, licensing and other categories increased 6.2 percent to $78.4 million.

Meredith Kopit Levien, the company’s chief executive, said in a statement that The Times’s “subscriber growth was powered by strong engagement and retention,” and that the company had increased its profit “while continuing to invest in growth areas like video.”

The Times had $1.26 billion in cash and marketable securities at the end of September. The company in September formally expressed interest in buying Letterboxd, a social platform for film lovers, The Times reported. (A spokeswoman declined to comment.)

For the fourth quarter, the company forecast an increase of 12 to 15 percent in digital-only subscription revenue compared with the same period a year ago, and a high-single-digit to low-double-digit increase in digital advertising revenue. It also forecast a year-over-year increase of 6 to 8 percent in adjusted operating costs in the fourth quarter.

item.title: A Lawsuit Says the McRib Is Lacking Something You Might Expect It to Have
item.description:
Judges make important rulings every day. They decide guilt or innocence, the length of prison terms and the resolution of multimillion-dollar lawsuits.

Last week, Judge April M. Perry ruled in United States District Court in Chicago that a class-action lawsuit against McDonald’s over its McRib sandwich could proceed.

The lawsuit claims that McDonald’s is misleading consumers. Why? Because the McRib isn’t made from rib meat.

The meat in a McRib is pressed into a shape that resembles a small rack of ribs. And “rib” is right there in the name. But rib meat, which is pricier than other parts of a pig, is nowhere to be found.

McDonald’s says on its website that the meat is “seasoned boneless pork.” In 2013, it acknowledged to ABC News that the meat was pork shoulder. The lawsuit contends that additional parts of the pig are used as well.

The lawsuit accuses McDonald’s of “deliberate sleight of hand.” It asks for unspecified monetary damages and calls on the company to “desist from further naming, marketing and advertising practices” that it says have misled consumers.

McDonald’s noted there was a “Mc” before the word “rib” in the sandwich’s name to identify the product as being from the company. But Judge Perry, ruling that the suit could proceed, said that “the alleged problem is not the prefix but the suffix.”

The judge noted that while the McChicken sandwich contains chicken, the pattern does not remain true for every McDonald’s product. “Dinosaur nuggets did not contain dinosaur meat,” she wrote, “and the McFlurry does not come accompanied by a small snowstorm.”

Still, she wrote, “on the spectrum of literal to symbolic, the McRib is arguably much closer to the literal, given that rib meat actually exists in a way that dinosaur meat and tiny snowstorms in a cup do not.”

McDonalds said in a statement in January, when the suit was filed, that “this lawsuit distorts the facts and the claims are meritless.”

“Our fan-favorite McRib sandwich is made with 100 percent pork sourced from farmers and suppliers across the U.S.,” the company said. “There are no hearts, tripe or scalded stomach used in the McRib patty as falsely alleged in this lawsuit.”

A lawyer for the plaintiffs, Thiago Coelho, said, “We will continue fighting for consumers who were misled and seeking accountability for deceptive marketing.”

The McRib, which debuted in 1981, has developed something of a cult following over the years, stoked by its limited availability. Generally, It turns up only in the fall and only at some locations, leading fans to share details of where to find it on websites like the McRib Locator.

The sandwich, which also includes onions and pickles, is more expensive than most of the other offerings on the McDonald’s menu, selling for up to $8. The cost was brought up in the suit, which alleges that the price misleads consumers into thinking higher quality rib meat is involved.

The judge noted that allowing the suit to continue did not mean she agreed with the plaintiffs, just that their claim could be plausible. Some parts of the suit were dismissed, but most claims will go forward, for now.

“The court is not persuaded by defendant’s many arguments that it would be unreasonable or fanciful to think the McRib contains rib meat,” she wrote.

Kristen Noyes contributed research.

item.title: How Trump’s Energy Policies Helped Trigger Tuesday’s Election Rout
item.description:
President Trump spent much of the past two years promising to bring down energy prices.

Instead, his war with Iran, as well as other policies, drove up the cost of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time his administration worked to thwart efforts to fight climate change, blocking renewable energy investments that could have reduced the country’s reliance on fossil fuels or brought down costs.

On Tuesday, voters’ frustration with soaring energy prices helped propel Democrats to a blowout, with Republicans losing control of the House and the Senate, as well as the governorships of many historically conservative states.

“It’s quite clear that energy and energy affordability in particular played a big role in the electorate’s decision-making last night,” said Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a clean energy finance company.

Many Americans said concerns about the cost of gas and electricity informed their voting choices, according to polling from The Associated Press. Gasoline prices across the country were at a record high for an Election Day, according to AAA.

No single action had a bigger effect on energy costs than Mr. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. With the Strait of Hormuz closed and global flows of oil disrupted, gasoline prices in the United States have jumped more than 40 percent since the war began. Diesel prices are up nearly 70 percent.

Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said that launching the war was among the worst decisions Mr. Trump could have made if he was trying to bring down energy costs. “It’s Econ 101 that invading Iran when they control the Strait of Hormuz is going to impact gas prices,” she said.

Daniel Raimi, a fellow at Resources for the Future, a nonprofit research institute, noted that “usually presidents have very little sway over global oil prices, but that was not the case this time.” The Iran war, he said, not only increased fuel prices but also costs for fertilizer “and a whole host of commodities.”

Beyond the war in Iran, the Trump administration has taken a sweeping approach to reshaping the nation’s energy policy, including actions that may have increased costs for consumers.

At a time when electricity demand and prices are soaring because of the data center boom, the administration has blocked the construction of offshore wind farms, despite pleas from governors to allow the projects to get built. It also mandated that coal-burning power plans stay online, even though utilities said that doing so would raise prices for their customers.

Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said on Wednesday that higher energy costs were a factor with voters. “Some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous, but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs: on electricity, on health care, on goods,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump.

If there was one energy-related issue beyond Iran that broke through, Mr. Raimi said, it was likely higher electricity prices, which many Americans blame on the proliferation of data centers. “Voters are certainly unhappy about higher electricity bills, but the larger driver for those higher prices is increased demand,” he said.

While data centers have become deeply unpopular with voters, Mr. Trump and his administration have offered stalwart support for the industry and dismissed voters’ concerns about them.

Other issues, like keeping coal plants open or blocking wind farms, he said, were less important in the voting booth because their effect on prices would be marginal.

Some of the Democrats who won seized on energy affordability as part of their campaigns. Roy Cooper, who flipped a Republican Senate seat in North Carolina, said at a campaign stop that the war in Iran was “driving the cost of gas through the roof.”

James Talarico, who became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas in decades, has called for suspending the federal gas tax and diesel tax.

And Abdul El-Sayed, who won a Senate seat in Michigan, touted the need to adopt clean energy. “We have all the technology we need to drop the price of electricity via renewable energy,” he said at a recent event. “And all of those renewable energy investments, guess what? They create really great jobs.”

While Democrats will soon be in control of Congress, bringing down energy prices is unlikely to be swift or easy.

Mr. Trump has two years left in office. In recent weeks, he has indicated that he might intensify attacks in Iran following the midterm election, which could lead to further spikes in oil prices.

But with voters signaling their frustration with the high cost of gas, diesel and electricity, some clean-energy supporters said they believed even Mr. Trump might be open to revising his stance on some issues that have driven up prices.

“The election was a compete repudiation of his energy agenda,” said Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, an environmental group. “The question is what comes next, and one thing he could do is stop blocking clean power that could help meet demand and lower costs.”

item.title: Trump Administration Moves to Oust Arbitrators as Doctor Payouts Soar
item.description:
The federal government plans to end contracts with two arbitration firms that settle medical billing disputes under the No Surprises Act, a consumer protection law that has come under scrutiny for high payouts for doctors.

Congress passed the law in 2020 to protect patients from surprise bills when they saw a doctor who did not have a contract with their health plan, such as in emergencies. The law, which took effect in 2022, calls for health care providers and insurers to settle on a price and when they cannot, for arbitrators to review an offer from each side, and pick one.

When the law passed, its authors expected the system to be used rarely and decisions generally to be split between the sides. But doctors have flooded the system with millions of cases and have prevailed overwhelmingly, winning more than 85 percent of them in 2025, according to the most recent federal data. Many have received awards dozens of times higher than usual insurer rates.

One New York plastic surgery practice won $440,000 for breast reduction surgeries in arbitration, The New York Times previously reported, and a surgical assistant in New Jersey won $106,500 for assisting on lower back surgery.

The law has been a financial boon for the arbitration firms as well. The government contracts with 17 firms to handle the millions of cases that now flow through the arbitration process. The arbitrators set their own fees, earning $425 to $800 for each dispute they settle, and they have collectively earned $742 million between 2022 and 2025.

While the contractors are all supposed to follow the same rules, federal data shows that outcomes vary dramatically between the arbitrators.

The Trump administration plans to cancel contracts with the two highlighted firms.

Source: Turquoise Health

By The New York Times

Some outside experts have argued that, because the arbitrators are paid per case, they have an incentive to side with the doctors to keep them coming back to the system. Doctors appear to win their cases at similar rates when they request modest or huge payments.

Insurers, who have argued that the arbitrators frequently decide cases that should not even be eligible for the process, have declined to pay some awards.

The arbitrators’ contracts last five years, and the government is now reviewing those awarded in 2022.

Two firms, Island Peer Review Organization and Network Medical Review Company, were notified on Wednesday that the government does not plan to renew their contracts, according a notice published that day.

The notice did not say why the companies’ applications had been denied.

An FAQ document published this summer provided possible grounds for denial, which included application paperwork errors, a lack of staff training, conflicts of interest or a failure to decide cases accurately.

In a statement, Christopher Krepich, a spokesman for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees the program, said the firms’ applications had been denied for performance reasons.

“The departments determined that these entities did not substantially comply with the standards governing their performance during their current certification terms,” he said.

Neither firm was immediately available for comment.

Island Peer Review Organization had been finding in doctors’ favor 96.5 percent of the time, the highest of any arbitration firms, according to an analysis by the health data firm Turquoise. It has handled nearly 450,000 disputes through the end of last year, according to federal data.

That work had transformed the finances of the small Long Island nonprofit firm, increasing its revenues from $68 million in 2022 to $171 million in 2025, according to public tax filings, as Stat News reported.

Network Medical Review Company has handled 363,000 cases and sided with doctors in 70.8 percent of them, according to the Turquoise analysis. It is a privately held company, so information on its finances is not publicly available.

The firms have decided cases that were highlighted in Times reporting on the arbitration system. Network Medical Review Company awarded an assistant breast surgeon $220,000 for his work on a breast reduction surgery. (Another firm awarded the primary surgeon an additional $220,000 for the case.) Island Peer Review Organization awarded an assistant surgeon $50,000 for work on a prostate surgery, 27 times the fee paid to the main surgeon in the case.

In recent weeks, the administration has announced that eight other firms have met the initial criteria to earn another five-year contract. Some of those arbitrators have similar records of lopsided and high awards to medical providers. Others are still being reviewed.

The two firms losing contracts will have 30 days to dispute the government’s decision. The process must be completed by the end of the year.

The disparate win rates and high-dollar awards have caught the attention of Congress, where interest in revising the law is growing. Representative Frank Pallone Jr., Democrat of New Jersey, introduced legislation last month proposing to abolish the arbitration system entirely.

He has also opened an investigation into the arbitration firms, sending them detailed requests for information on how they make their decisions.

The Trump administration has also signaled some interest in reforms. “The system is being gamed to get higher prices, and C.M.S. is actively working to clean it up,” Mr. Krepich, the agency spokesman, told The Times in July.

This appears to be their first action to change the arbitration system.

item.title: Shares of Truth Social’s Parent Company Hit New Low
item.description:
President Trump’s social media company recorded one of its biggest daily market losses on Wednesday, a day after Democrats scored staggering victories in the midterm elections.

Shares of Trump Media & Technology Group plunged 24 percent to close at $4.49 — a low for the parent company of Truth Social.

On Wall Street, trading in shares of Trump Media have always been something of a proxy for Mr. Trump’s popularity. But the decline in Trump Media’s stock price has accelerated in recent months as its quarterly losses have mounted.

With the most recent sell-off, shares of Trump Media are down more than 90 percent from the closing price on the stock’s first day of trading, on March 26, 2024. Shortly after the company made its Wall Street debut, Mr. Trump’s stake in Trump Media was valued at around $6 billion. Now it is worth just over $500 million.

And there is a fresh concern for the company: newly empowered congressional Democrats with the ability to start investigations into business dealings involving Mr. Trump and his family.

One that could face scrutiny is Trump Media’s business of selling early access to Mr. Trump’s Truth Social posts to investment firms seeking to use the information to make lightning-fast trades. Immediately after Trump Media announced plans to offer this early access to the president’s posts, several congressional Democrats denounced it as giving an unfair advantage to some traders. Other Democratic lawmakers introduced a bill that would bar Trump Media from selling this early access.

A Trump Media spokesman declined to comment.

The precipitous fall in shares of Trump Media has left some early backers of the company frustrated and angry.

Chad Nedohin, a part-time pastor and oil and gas engineer who had been one of Trump Media’s biggest proponents online, feels betrayed. He said the company had strayed too far from its original mission of promoting a free speech platform for conservatives.

Mr. Nedohin, who has sold most of his shares, said he would like to see a securities lawyer bring a shareholder lawsuit. He said early investors were true believers in Truth Social and the company’s mission, and have been dismayed to see it constantly moving in different directions.

“The early shareholders did the right thing for the right reason, but it is devastating that Trump is not the person we thought,” Mr. Nedohin said.

There are other hurdles on the horizon. On Nov. 30, investors in a $1 billion bond offering have the option of redeeming their original investment from Trump Media, according to company regulatory filings. The debt offering, from 2025, helped fuel Trump Media’s $2 billion move into Bitcoin and crypto. It is unclear how many investors might choose to exercise that option.

At the moment, the company has at least $1.65 billion in cash, investments and digital assets.

And on Dec. 14, Trump Media shareholders will vote on the company’s proposed merger with TAE Technologies, a nuclear fusion technology company. TAE’s auditor has said the company, which still doesn’t have a commercially viable product, is on the verge of running out of money.

The deal is all but certain to be approved by Trump Media shareholders as Mr. Trump’s shares, which are held in a trust, are already pledged to vote for it. He is the company’s largest shareholder.

item.title: White House Delays Hearing on Fed Governor
item.description:
The White House is rescheduling its planned hearing on Thursday with Lisa D. Cook, the Federal Reserve governor whom President Trump has tried to fire over unproven allegations of mortgage fraud.

The hearing is now set for Dec. 14, according to a White House official. The move came days after Ms. Cook’s lawyers said she could not participate on Nov. 5 because of schedule conflicts.

Lawyers for Ms. Cook did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Her lawyers have raised a litany of concerns about the investigation, which is being overseen by three of the president’s political appointees.

The high-stakes battle for the Fed began last year, after Mr. Trump and his top aides claimed that Ms. Cook had misrepresented her finances in order to obtain more favorable mortgage terms. She has denied the charges, which have never been brought in court.

The president still attempted to oust Ms. Cook from her Senate-confirmed post, a move that stoked widespread opposition out of concern that Mr. Trump could politicize the Fed, a politically independent institution that sets the nation’s monetary policy. It coincided with a parallel effort by the president to pressure the central bank into lowering interest rates.

Ultimately, the Supreme Court blocked Mr. Trump in June, after the justices found that the White House did not afford Ms. Cook a full opportunity to respond to the allegations. But even in defeat, the president did not back down, setting in motion a monthslong effort by the administration to try again.

In October, the president commissioned a special panel to investigate the matter and report back on whether there would be grounds for “Governor Cook’s removal.” The committee appeared to be calibrated in a way to address the justices’ concerns, though Mr. Trump stocked its members with three allies and deputies.

As a result, Ms. Cook’s lawyers then raised “significant concerns” over the “objectivity and fitness of the committee,” given the president’s past threats and the actions and comments of the panel’s members.

item.title: The Making of Dario Amodei
item.description:
One night in 2007, Dario Amodei regaled a friend who was visiting him at Princeton University with his thoughts on “The Singularity Is Near,” a 2005 treatise by the computer scientist Ray Kurzweil.

Dr. Amodei had just read the book, in which Mr. Kurzweil predicted that artificial intelligence would eventually surpass the human brain in a moment known as the Singularity. As he twisted his hair with his fingers, Dr. Amodei told his friend, Colin Heckman, that the milestone could happen within their lifetimes.

“He became obsessed,” said Mr. Heckman, who went to high school with Dr. Amodei in San Francisco. “He said A.I. had to be built right, or we’re going to be done.”

Dr. Amodei, then 24 and a doctoral student in physics, was in a period of soaking up information. He had become absorbed in the obscure blogs “Accelerating Future” and “Overcoming Bias,” where writers discussed A.I.’s potential to wipe out humanity. And he had delved into the online forums of GiveWell, an organization that aimed to maximize the effectiveness of charitable giving, where intellectuals debated how to make the most money for philanthropy.

These books, blogs and online communities have influenced Dr. Amodei to this day, according to interviews with more than two dozen of his classmates, friends, teachers and colleagues. They help explain the ideas that drive the 43-year-old chief executive of Anthropic, a company that is set to conduct one of the world’s largest public listings this month, and offer an understanding of how the man at the forefront of the A.I. revolution actually thinks about A.I.

At the heart of Dr. Amodei’s worldview, his friends and colleagues said, are two interwoven philosophies that share an uncompromising belief that mathematical reasoning can change the future of humanity.

One is “rationalism,” which aims to apply dispassionate thinking to the world. Espoused by people like Eliezer Yudkowsky, a self-taught A.I. researcher, it argues that A.I. will become powerful enough to destroy society. The other is “effective altruism,” which evolved alongside rationalism and seeks to maximize social good with mathematical precision.

These schools of thought fused for Dr. Amodei into an unyielding conviction that A.I. could be so dangerous that only he and like-minded technologists could be entrusted with building it. That catalyzed his stated efforts to create A.I. before people without concerns about the safety of humanity did, and spurred a desire to control the technology, his friends and colleagues said.

With A.I., “the benefits will only be achieved if we build the technology in the right way, and — so long as we use the time we gain well — it is worth taking unusually deliberate care to get it right,” Dr. Amodei wrote in a September essay that called for a slowdown in the technology’s development.

These ideas formed the foundation for Anthropic, which Dr. Amodei established in 2021 with his sister, Daniela Amodei, and five others who spent time around rationalist and effective altruist communities. And as the company sprouted, their views — which Dr. Amodei has pushed vocally and relentlessly — have become increasingly prominent.

Dr. Amodei has weighed in on geopolitical debates and said the United States should restrict chip sales to China to limit that nation from competing in A.I. He has proclaimed that A.I. should be regulated to stop the technology from going rogue. And in disputes with the Department of Defense, he has declared that the technology should not be used for the mass surveillance of Americans or deployed in autonomous weapons.

“He actually sees that there’s a huge existential risk on the table here,” said Nathan Avery, who ran high school cross-country with Dr. Amodei and had many deep conversations with him over the years, though they have drifted apart. “And he needs to put himself in a position to do something about it.”

Dr. Amodei, a billionaire whose net worth is set to grow with Anthropic’s public offering, declined through a company representative to be interviewed.

His thinking has won him supporters, especially among some who work in A.I. safety and who say Dr. Amodei is developing A.I. responsibly. It has also made him enemies in Silicon Valley and Washington, with critics — including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang — attacking him for being a “doomer” and trying to centralize power in A.I. In September, the Defense Department posted on social media: “Americanism, not effective altruism.”

Dr. Amodei, who appears to be aware that his ideas have riled others, has tried to publicly differentiate his beliefs from rationalism and effective altruism. In 2023, he told The New York Times’s “Hard Fork” podcast that he did not consider himself to be an effective altruist.

“I’m sympathetic to a number of the ideas,” he said, but against “dividing people up into tribes.”

Dr. Amodei and his younger sister Daniela grew up in San Francisco’s Mission District. Their father, Riccardo Amodei, was a leather craftsman, and their mother, Elena Engel, managed public library renovations. The couple separated in 1991, according to divorce filings.

By eighth grade at Lawton Alternative School, Dr. Amodei stood out. In 1997, he and a peer were voted “Most Likely to Succeed” and were pictured in their yearbook holding dollar bills.

At Lowell High School, San Francisco’s top public high school, Dr. Amodei was a voracious learner who took classes at the University of California, Berkeley. He pondered ideas like utilitarianism, which argues that people should maximize happiness for the most living beings, and worried about issues like the Y2K bug and its potential to ruin the world’s computers, classmates said.

Richard Shapiro, then a physics teacher at Lowell, said Dr. Amodei had frequently thought he underperformed on tests. “I’d yell at him, ‘Dario, lighten up!’” Mr. Shapiro said.

In 2001, Dr. Amodei enrolled at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, but often returned to San Francisco to see friends and family. On one trip, he went with Mr. Avery and Mr. Heckman to a sushi restaurant, where they debated utilitarianism. Dr. Amodei was a vegetarian but argued it was fine to eat crabs because they are invertebrates.

During the meal, Mr. Heckman presented a thought experiment: If someone started killing as many chickens as possible, when would it make sense to kill that person to prevent more chickens from dying? Dr. Amodei chuckled, then said that “there was some number of chickens that would outweigh a human in the utilitarian sense,” Mr. Avery recalled.

Mr. Amodei has said he is an atheist, but he still had strong convictions, his friends said. In 2003, he drove Mr. Avery and others to protests in San Francisco against the U.S. invasion of Iraq.

The next year, Dr. Amodei transferred to Stanford University, in the heart of Silicon Valley. The move brought him closer to Ms. Amodei, who was in high school nearby.

“We always wanted to save the world together,” he said of his sister on a 2023 podcast.

After graduating from Stanford in 2006, Dr. Amodei joined a physics doctoral program at Princeton, eventually focusing on applying physics to biology and computational neuroscience. That year, his father, who suffered from hepatitis C, died. Dr. Amodei threw himself into researching retina cells and became interested in developing technology to accelerate scientific progress.

Jade Wang, who dated Dr. Amodei and started a science discussion group with him, said they had often talked about how scientists who dedicated their lives to studying one disease would have a greater impact developing technology or methods for their entire field. He cited his father, who died before the discovery of a drug that made most hepatitis C cases treatable, she said.

By then, Dr. Amodei was embracing the writings of Mr. Kurzweil and Mr. Yudkowsky, a leader of the rationalists. He was especially intrigued by Mr. Kurzweil’s idea that advanced technologies would let humans exist beyond natural limits, a belief known as transhumanism.

During Mr. Heckman’s 2007 visit to Princeton, Dr. Amodei told him that the Singularity would happen by 2040 and that humans might someday meld their minds with machines. “We would over time become the new superintelligent A.I. or A.I.-human hybrid,” Dr. Amodei said, according to Mr. Heckman.

Dr. Amodei became so fascinated by this thinking that he encouraged his friends and sister to attend the annual conference of Mr. Yudkowsky’s Singularity Institute. (The group is now called the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.)

Mr. Yudkowsky was “one of the deepest thinkers I have ever encountered” and “explicitly trying to bring about a singularity that will be beneficial to humanity,” Dr. Amodei told friends in a 2008 email seen by The Times.

In an email to The Times, Mr. Yudkowsky said Dr. Amodei “does not currently ask or take my advice and I do not remember any time when he did.”

Around then, Dr. Amodei also began corresponding with Elon Musk, who had founded the rocket company SpaceX. Dr. Amodei told friends that he admired the tech mogul and had considered working for him, but he never did at the space start-up, two people with knowledge of the men’s communications said.

In 2008, Dr. Amodei came across GiveWell while reading the blog of the economist Tyler Cowen, who posted that the organization offered “interesting tips” on charities. Dr. Amodei became active on GiveWell’s email lists and forums, where he discussed an effective altruist approach to philanthropy and science.

In 2010, he wrote that he was “considering a career in finance, which would allow me to give away more money than I currently do,” according to an email seen by The Times.

In a blog post for GiveWell that year, Dr. Amodei discussed a decision to give away $10,000. He was choosing to donate to either the Stop TB Partnership, which focused on preventing adult tuberculosis, or VillageReach, which helped vaccinate children in African villages.

The Stop TB Partnership, Dr. Amodei wrote, was superior in “cost-effectiveness” because it served adults and “adults are capable of deeper and more meaningful experiences” than infants. “I think an adult death is perhaps 2 or 3 times worse than an infant’s death,” he added.

Dr. Amodei ultimately changed his mind after considering how the groups executed their missions and deeming VillageReach to be more effective.

In 2011, he started postdoctoral work at Stanford studying cancer cells. In his personal life, he experimented with anti-aging supplements, maintained a strict swimming regimen and became interested caloric reduction, which was shown in some studies to prolong the lives of lab mice, his friends said.

“He would often talk about the finiteness of time and how it was the one nonrenewable resource,” Mr. Avery said, adding that Dr. Amodei was “ruthless with his time.”

That was compounded by a diagnosis for testicular cancer in 2014, two people who know him said. Dr. Amodei underwent chemotherapy and made a full recovery.

By then, he had become close to Holden Karnofsky, a GiveWell founder. GiveWell had started working with Good Ventures, the philanthropy of the Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and his wife, Cari Tuna, who finance effective altruist causes. Dr. Amodei began advising the partnership, GiveWell Labs, on life sciences funding.

At the time, Mr. Karnofsky was dating Ms. Amodei. The couple moved into a group house in San Francisco, which eventually included Dr. Amodei; Jared Kaplan, a theoretical physicist; and Christopher Olah, a college dropout who had been tutored in math by Dr. Amodei.

The housemates discussed Mr. Yudkowsky’s essays and explored rationalism and effective altruism, three people who visited the home said. They also attended Burning Man, the annual counterculture gathering in the Nevada desert, sometimes dressing up in animal costumes.

Dr. Kaplan and Mr. Olah later co-founded Anthropic with Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei. In 2025, Mr. Karnofsky also started working for the company.

In the early 2010s, advancements in machine learning — computer algorithms that learn to perform tasks on their own by analyzing data — led to new investments by tech companies in A.I.

One company that jumped in was the Chinese internet giant Baidu, which opened a lab in Sunnyvale, Calif., and hired an A.I. pioneer, Andrew Ng, from Google as chief scientist. Dr. Amodei joined Baidu in 2014 and quickly became known for staying overnight at the office and sharing his opinions.

“Dario argued very aggressively at pretty much every opportunity,” said Gregory Diamos, a researcher who worked with Dr. Amodei at Baidu.

Even in the early days of this A.I. period, Dr. Amodei was struck by the technology’s potential dangers. He told colleagues in 2015 that A.I. could soon match or exceed the abilities of the human brain, so companies developing it should not shy away from the possibility of its going awry, Dr. Diamos recalled.

That same year, Dr. Amodei joined a Google A.I. lab called Google Brain, where he focused on A.I. safety. He and five other researchers — including his housemate Mr. Olah — published a 2016 paper, “Concrete Problems in A.I. Safety,” which laid out how the technology could misbehave if it was wrongly developed.

In 2016, Dr. Amodei joined a new A.I. effort: a nonprofit called OpenAI. He led its safety team and another team that studied “scaling laws,” or the idea that A.I. models become more capable as they are trained with more data.

(The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

At OpenAI, Dr. Amodei’s beliefs on the correct way to develop A.I. hardened, seven people who worked with him said. He became more vocal about A.I.’s power and potential harms and acted to infuse the technology’s development with his thinking.

Three days after Donald J. Trump was elected president in November 2016, for instance, Dr. Amodei wrote in OpenAI’s internal messaging app that he was concerned the United States was sliding toward authoritarianism. He said he was “not comfortable conducting research on militarily powerful technologies in an authoritarian country,” according to messages seen by The Times.

Dr. Amodei also wrote that the investor Peter Thiel, who had donated $1.25 million to Mr. Trump’s campaign, was “morally worthy of condemnation” for that support and that OpenAI should no longer accept his money, according to internal messages. (Founders Fund, a venture capital firm started by Mr. Thiel, later invested in Anthropic.)

Dr. Amodei also helped arrange a deal between OpenAI and funders who aligned with his thinking. In 2017, he connected OpenAI to the philanthropy run by Mr. Karnofsky, for which Dr. Amodei was a technical adviser, three people familiar with the arrangement said.

Mr. Karnofsky’s organization, now known as Coefficient Giving, donated $30 million to OpenAI. Mr. Karnofsky also joined OpenAI’s board.

Later that year, Mr. Karnofsky and Ms. Amodei married. At their wedding, guests received stuffed animals and were rewarded for arranging “the most romantic hookups between the different characters,” according to the couple’s wedding website.

Dr. Amodei wore a panda head to the wedding, where the dress code for the reception was “silly formal.” In a photo viewed by The Times, he appeared in costume alongside Mr. Olah, who wore a giraffe head, and Cami Clark, a woman Dr. Amodei was dating. He and Ms. Clark married in 2022.

In 2018, Daniela Amodei joined OpenAI, eventually becoming vice president of safety and policy. Some employees soon raised questions about the siblings’ growing influence.

That December, Joshua Achiam, an OpenAI researcher, told Sam Altman, the chief executive, that it would be unwise to name Dr. Amodei the company’s chief ethics officer, three people with knowledge of the discussions said. Mr. Achiam cited the Amodeis’ increasing power and said A.I. oversight should be shared by people with different perspectives.

When Mr. Achiam insisted that an outside expert be named chief ethics officer, Dr. Amodei confronted him. Dr. Amodei raised his voice and said no one was better suited for the position than him, the people said.

In 2018, Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei took over a company project called GPT, short for generative pre-trained transformer. They explored a safety technique that aimed to teach A.I. to perform tasks with human instruction, six people who worked at the company said.

This approach — pushing A.I. closer to potential dangers and then testing it with safety techniques — would come to define Dr. Amodei’s career.

Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, tried to help with GPT. But Dr. Amodei and Ms. Amodei resisted, two people with knowledge of the company said. Dr. Amodei repeatedly told Mr. Altman that if he did not keep Mr. Brockman away from the work, he would leave, the people said.

For Mr. Altman, the ultimatums went too far, a person with knowledge of his thinking said. He refused the Amodeis’ demands.

In December 2020, Dr. Amodei, Ms. Amodei and other colleagues quit OpenAI. Four weeks later, they started Anthropic.

item.title: Life Is Funny. These Readers Drew Cartoons That Prove It.
item.description:
In the moment, it’s rarely funny: the waistband that splits, the machine that refuses to cooperate, the routine conversation that takes an unexpected turn. But with a little distance, even life’s small indignities can become a source of amusement.

When we invited readers to submit single-panel cartoons in the spirit of P.C. Vey, the longtime New Yorker cartoonist who died recently, we received more than 200 submissions.

The cartoonists found humor in the everyday absurdities of being human, our uneasy relationship with the modern world and our often futile efforts to improve ourselves. Many of the cartoons were clever and visually striking, and plenty made us laugh out loud.

We also asked Mr. Vey’s wife, Tina, what she thought of them. She liked one about the perils of saving for retirement and another about the simple pleasure of avoiding people.

“They had the essence of Peter,” she said by phone.

Below is a selection.

The world doesn’t always make sense. Fortunately, neither do we.

Technology was meant to make life easier. So why doesn’t it feel that way?

We’re all trying to get somewhere: to become more accomplished, more organized, more enlightened, more stylish. But the road to becoming our best selves, it turns out, has a few potholes.

item.title: China Blocks SoftBank’s $5.4 Billion Robotics Takeover, Impeding Foreign Deals
item.description:
​Chinese authorities thwarted a multibillion-dollar effort by the Japanese tech giant SoftBank to expand further into robotics, showing Beijing’s willingness to intervene in global business deals that may impact its own technology ambitions.

On Thursday, ABB, a Swiss-Swedish industrial company, said that the sale of its robotics division to SoftBank for $5.4 billion, which was announced last year, had been blocked by a Chinese regulator that conducts national security reviews of foreign investments.

China’s approval was needed for the SoftBank acquisition to move ahead in part because so much of ABB’s sales come from the country. At a factory in Shanghai, ABB produces a variety of products, mainly used for manufacturing and automating tasks like handling heavy materials and polishing.

China is taking an aggressive approach to reviewing foreign deals involving key technology and sensitive industries. In April, regulators forced Meta to unwind its $2 billion acquisition of the Chinese A.I. start-up Manus.

To block the Manus deal, authorities cited national security concerns, a move seen as signaling the government’s determination to keep important technology and talented engineers from being acquired by foreign companies.

China’s scrutiny of foreign deals is raising concerns about operating in the country as technology development takes on more strategic importance in government planning. Regulators in the United States, European Union and Britain have also intervened in deals involving semiconductors, quantum computing and other technology.

ABB, based in Zurich, has decades-long ties to Chinese manufacturing businesses, which gives it access to valuable data on robotics technology. China is ABB’s largest robotics market and about 90 percent of its machines built for Chinese customers are manufactured locally. The company employs thousands of people in the country.

Chinese authorities were concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas and used to train A.I. models, according to The Financial Times, which first reported that the deal was blocked.

China’s intervention is a major blow to SoftBank and its founder, Masayoshi Son, one of the tech industry’s biggest believers in artificial intelligence. He has staked his company’s future on the technology and has viewed robots as the essential link between the technology and the physical world.

Yet concerns have grown that Mr. Son has put too much emphasis on A.I. SoftBank has invested roughly $65 billion in OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and billions more into data center businesses.

On Thursday, shares of SoftBank fell almost 7 percent and are down nearly 30 percent over the past year. The Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday also hit the shares of some big tech firms, as many of the winning governors and legislators have pushed for stricter oversight of the A.I. build-out, which could slow its expansion.

A spokesman for SoftBank did not respond to messages seeking comment.

item.title: High Gas Prices Boost Sales for Hybrid Giant Toyota, Sending Stock Soaring
item.description:
Rising gasoline prices are steering American car buyers toward hybrid vehicles, delivering a windfall for their biggest producer, Toyota Motor.

Toyota said on Thursday that it expected its operating profit to rise to $24.7 billion for the current year through March, up 15 percent from its previous forecast. The automaker also reported higher earnings between April and September, buoyed by rising hybrid sales in the United States.

The results pushed Toyota’s shares up more than 16 percent in Tokyo on Thursday. It was the company’s biggest daily gain in nearly 40 years.

Toyota’s strong earnings underscore how the company’s once contrarian bet on hybrid vehicles is paying off, as high gas prices from the war in the Middle East push American drivers toward more fuel-efficient cars — just not fully electric ones.

In the third quarter, total hybrid vehicle sales in the United States rose 28 percent from the same period a year prior. Sales of electric vehicles declined 40 percent, as the Trump administration’s elimination of federal tax credits continued to sap demand.

For now, in the United States, “inventories of hybrid vehicles are extremely tight — essentially, they sell like hot cakes even without discounting,” said Sanshiro Fukao, an executive fellow at the Itochu Research Institute. “That dynamic is very strong, and is by far the biggest driver behind Toyota’s strong earnings,” he said.

Toyota said on Thursday that it sold 2.36 million hybrid vehicles during the April-through-September period, an 8 percent increase from the same period a year earlier. The profit it makes from the vehicles has also been bolstered by the weakness of the yen, which inflates the value of its overseas earnings.

In the early 2020s, when much of the automotive industry moved rapidly to focus on electric vehicles, Toyota stood behind its wager that hybrid demand would endure. At the time, rivals such as Honda Motor, which pledged to phase out gasoline engines entirely by 2040, became darlings of investors and other groups that were bullish on all things E.V.

Now, the shift in the market has set many automakers back. Honda posted the first annual net loss in its seven-decade history in May, after taking on billions in restructuring charges and write-downs related to a retrenchment of its E.V. strategy. Volkswagen said in September that it would cut roughly 50,000 additional jobs in the face of costs related to E.V.s and rising competition in China.

Toyota is not immune to the challenges faced by its competitors. Chinese automakers have begun flooding global markets with inexpensive electric cars, and foreign automakers are being squeezed in China, the world’s biggest auto market. Toyota’s sales in the country fell by a quarter during the April-through-September period, reaching their lowest level in nearly a decade.

The question now is whether the tide in the U.S. electric vehicle market could turn once more. With Democrats regaining control of both the Senate and the House in this week’s midterm elections, a renewed legislative push for pro-E.V. policies has become far more likely, Mr. Fukao said.

“Toyota’s current stellar earnings could be considered quite short-term,” Mr. Fukao said. “While hybrids currently account for strong sales, the looming question of how the Japanese auto industry will fare once we have to compete on battery E.V.s again could undeniably become a major challenge.”
